title: Tetraplegic man controls a four-limb exoskeleton and avatar through an adaptive epidural ECoG decoder at Clinatec, Grenoble
summary: A 28-year-old with C4-C5 tetraplegia cortically controlled simulated walking and 8-DoF arm movements over 24 months (Lancet Neurology 2019).
account: A 28-year-old man with tetraplegia after a C4-C5 spinal cord injury was implanted at the Clinatec research centre of the French Alternative Energies and Atomic Energy Commission (CEA), associated with Grenoble University Hospital, with two wireless epidural recorders of 64 electrodes each over the sensorimotor cortex. Epidural electrocorticographic signals were processed online by an adaptive decoding algorithm that sent commands to a virtual avatar or a four-limb exoskeleton. Between 12 June 2017 and 21 July 2019 he cortically controlled a programme that simulated walking and made bimanual upper-limb movements with eight degrees of freedom, with 64.0% success using the avatar at home and 70.9% with the exoskeleton in the laboratory; decoding models were reusable for about seven weeks without recalibration (Lancet Neurology, 2019).
purpose: Restore mobility to people with tetraplegia by decoding brain signals to drive an exoskeleton
system: Clinatec epidural wireless brain-machine interface with adaptive decoder driving a four-limb exoskeleton and virtual avatar
developer: CEA-Clinatec (public research institute, not a company) with Grenoble University Hospital
deployer: Clinatec research centre / Grenoble University Hospital clinical trial
taxonomy_note: Closest fit; the gain is brain-controlled movement of an exoskeleton in a proof-of-concept setting.

ratings.reason: One identifiable participant gained brain-controlled walking simulation and eight-degree-of-freedom arm control, exercised at home with an avatar and in the laboratory with the exoskeleton; it did not yet provide everyday mobility, so -3 is not supported.
Single-patient proof of concept for semi-invasive long-term BCI; no population effect.

ai_role.statement: The adaptive decoding algorithm (later described by the same group as a recursive exponentially weighted Markov-switching multilinear mixture-of-experts model) is the component that converts epidural ECoG into effector commands; without it the implants record only. The exoskeleton itself was ceiling-suspended in the laboratory.

evidence.citation: Benabid AL, Costecalde T, Eliseyev A, et al. (2019). An exoskeleton controlled by an epidural wireless brain-machine interface in a tetraplegic patient: a proof-of-concept demonstration. Lancet Neurology 18(12):1112-1122.
evidence.title: An exoskeleton controlled by an epidural wireless brain-machine interface in a tetraplegic patient: a proof-of-concept demonstration
evidence.quote: Epidural electrocorticographic (ECoG) signals were processed online by an adaptive decoding algorithm to send commands to effectors (virtual avatar or exoskeleton).

evidence.citation: Benabid AL, et al. (2019). Lancet Neurology 18(12):1112-1122 (findings).
evidence.title: An exoskeleton controlled by an epidural wireless brain-machine interface in a tetraplegic patient (findings)
evidence.quote: the patient cortically controlled a programme that simulated walking and made bimanual, multi-joint, upper-limb movements with eight degrees of freedom during various reach-and-touch tasks

evidence.citation: Moly A, Costecalde T, Martel F, et al. (2022). An adaptive closed-loop ECoG decoder for long-term and stable bimanual control of an exoskeleton by a tetraplegic. Journal of Neural Engineering 19(2).
evidence.title: An adaptive closed-loop ECoG decoder for long-term and stable bimanual control of an exoskeleton by a tetraplegic
evidence.quote: The stable over a period of six months (without decoder recalibration) eight-dimensional alternative bimanual control of the exoskeleton and its virtual avatar is demonstrated.

produced_by: Chronic bilateral epidural ECoG recorders with wireless transmission
Adaptive, incrementally trained decoder with idle-state support
Progressive training on mental tasks over 24 months
must_hold: Stable epidural signal quality over years
Decoder recalibration roughly every seven weeks
Laboratory suspension system for safe exoskeleton walking

echoes.setting: Same patient, more than 36 months after implantation, asynchronous bimanual exoskeleton control
echoes.source: Moly et al. (2022) J Neural Eng, PMID 35234665

headline: Clinatec's ECoG decoder drives a four-limb exoskeleton
metric: 64.0% success using the avatar at home and 70.9% with the exoskeleton in the laboratory
